newsitem.title: BAHAMAS: Hurricane Hortense moving quickly to the north.
newsitem.headline: Hurricane Hortense moving quickly to the north.

text.p: Hurricane Hortense moved briskly across the open Atlantic Ocean on Friday after causing floods in Puerto Rico and the Dominican Republic that killed about two dozen people.

Hortense's maximum sustained winds weakened overnight to 125 mph (200 km) and the storm was downgraded to a still dangerous Category Three hurricane. While the storm remained far out in the Atlantic, forecasters said heavy swells could reach the East Coast and Bermuda Friday and Saturday.

Forecasters said Hortense was not expected to strike the U.S. mainland because of a cold weather front pushing it north, although there was an outside chance it might brush Cape Cod, Massachusetts, this weekend.

Some of the tiny southern islands in the long Bahamas archipelago were pelted with rain and gusty winds as Hortense moved past. The airport on the southeastern island of San Salvador was shut down until Saturday.

At 5 a.m. EDT (0900 GMT), Hortense's center was at latitude 28.1 north and longitude 71.2 west, about 560 miles (900 km) south-southeast of Cape Hatteras, North Carolina, and was moving quickly north at 20 miles (32 km), the National Hurricane Center said.

The hurricane was expected to keep moving toward the north then turn toward the north-northeast, a track that would keep it away from land until moving into the cool waters of the north Atlantic, where it would weaken sometime this weekend, forecasters said.

Hortense's official death toll in Puerto Rico reached 14 on Thursday, mostly from raging floods and mudslides, with the discovery of two more bodies, police said. Up to eight people were still missing, officially.
One of the bodies recovered on Thursday was the last member of a family of six, all of whom were killed when raging river waters swept away their home in the southeastern town of Guayama.
"We're expecting the number of dead and missing to rise," said police spokeswoman Maribel Hernandez. "We are just now getting into towns that were inaccessible."

A spokesman for the Puerto Rico Civil Defense said there were 7,864 people still in shelters. He said 35 percent of the island remained without power and 34 percent lacked potable water by Thursday, three days after Hortense arrived.
President Bill Clinton declared Puerto Rico a disaster area on Wednesday.

The death toll in the Dominican Republic also seemed likely to rise. The official figure was eight, but the Civil Defense reported 12 people missing in the northeastern coastal region brushed by Hortense.
"They are searching and I must admit that the situation in the region is certainly critical," said Eugenio Cabral, director of the Civil Defense.
One of the dead in San Rafael de Yuna, a coastal village near La Romana, was a 17-day-old baby, according to a fire department spokesman.

Three provinces -- Altagracia, Nagua and Samana -- were declared to be in a state of emergency as swollen rivers burst out of their banks and sent flood waters down mountains and valleys. "Entire families have disappeared," said Amable Aristy Castro, president of the Dominican Senate.
After leaving the Dominican Republic, Hortense passed the low-lying Turks and Caicos Islands, a British colony of about 13,000 residents, overnight on its way to the Bahamas.
Officials in the Turks and Caicos said damage was essentially limited to minor roof failures and downed utility poles and that no casualties had been reported.

"Life is almost back to normal, everybody's cleaning up this morning and waiting for the restoration of electricity," said law office worker Cheryl Francis-Faessler on Grand Turk, which lies at the east end of the chain.
